### D.2 Teachers and trajectory data

For each of the six environments we distill a single Soft Actor-Critic [4] teacher policy trained by the Minari team [23].

Each teacher is rolled out for $T=2{,}000{,}000$ time steps in its environment using a fixed seed and the deterministic action mode. The resulting trajectory $(o_{t},a_{t})_{t=0}^{T-1}$ is the only data the student ever sees: no rollouts of the student itself appear in the training distribution. From this trajectory we construct a sliding-window supervised dataset

$$ \mathcal{D}\;=\;\big\{\,\big((o_{t-m+1:t},\,a_{t-m:t-1}),\;a_{t}\big)\,:\,t=m,\dots,T-1\,\big\}, $$

in which the student observes a length- $m$ window of past observations and previous actions at each time step and is trained, with mean-squared error against the teacher’s action $a_{t}$ , to predict the next action. We do not subsample or shuffle the trajectory, so the entire $T-m$ samples are used as training data for every student.

The “test” set in this experiment is the live environment itself: trained students are deployed deterministically and evaluated on $N_{\mathrm{eval}}=100$ episodes per checkpoint. We report best-checkpoint reward, defined as the mean episode reward of the checkpoint that achieves the highest mean reward over its $1{,}000$ deployment episodes. We save checkpoints every 5 epochs. Each episode runs to the environment’s default time limit or natural termination under the standard -v5 reward function.

### D.3 Shared encoder, head, and action squash

To isolate the effect of the sequence-mixing block from the surrounding architecture, all three students share an identical encoder and decoder architecture with embedding dimension $d$ that depends on the environment, (see Table 6).

- • Encoder ( $\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}+d_{a}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ): a two-layer GELU MLP applied independently at each time step. Both hidden layers have width $d$ , no normalization layers, and GELU is applied between the two linear layers. The encoder concatenates the current observation with the previous action before applying the MLP, so each time step in the sliding window contributes a single $d$ -dimensional embedding to the sequence-mixing block’s input.

- • Sequence-mixing block ( $\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ): the only component that varies across the three students. It consumes the length- $m$ sequence of encoder embeddings and produces a single $d$ -dimensional summary. The three variants are detailed in Appendix D.4.

- • Decoder ( $\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}$ ): a three-layer GELU MLP with first layer $d$ , second layer $d/2$ , and output $d_{a}$ , with GELU between layers and a final tanh normalization and scaling to ensure the student’s predictions live in the valid action box.

The only architectural variation across the three students lies in the sequence-mixing block.

### D.4 Sequence-mixing-block variants

The three students differ only in their sequence-mixing block.

#### STU (the train-then-distill variant).

At training time, the block is a tensor-dot Spectral Transform Unit [10] with $k=16$ spectral filters. We use the tensor-dot variant for parameter efficiency at $d=128$ ; Appendix F compares it against the STU on the linear-LDS task. At evaluation time, the trained STU is converted to a Diagonal LDS via SpectraLDS, and the converted Diagonal LDS is what we deploy. To allow for easier reuse of the published SpectraLDS conversions [17], we use the spectral filters computed with $m=8192$ and $k=48$ and at $80$ -dimensions, truncate, and consider the relevant subset of $k=16$ filters. The STU runs in float64 precision due to historical reasons, while other models are in the native float32. Based on later experimentation, we do not expect this contributes to any differences.

#### Diagonal LDS, $C$ -matched ( $h=d$ ).

A directly-trained recurrence $x_{t+1}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda)\,x_{t}+Bu_{t},\ y_{t}=Cx_{t}$ , with $\lambda=\tanh(\tilde{\lambda})\,(1-10^{-3})$ to keep eigenvalues strictly inside the unit disk.

#### Diagonal LDS, parameter-matched.

Identical to the $C$ -matched variant in form, but with $h$ chosen so that $h(1+2d)=2kd+d^{2}$ , giving exactly the same parameter count as STU’s tensor-dot block. This is the parameter-matched baseline for the train-then-distill comparison.

## Appendix F STU vs. tensor-dot STU

Both STU variants begin from the same intermediate object. Given an input window $x\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}$ and the fixed spectral filters $\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ , the spectrally-filtered representation of the window is the matrix

$$ Z\;=\;\phi^{\top}x\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad Z_{k,i}\;=\;\big\langle\phi_{:,k},\;x_{:,i}\big\rangle. $$

$Z$ has one row per spectral filter and one column per input channel; all of the time-window information that the predictor will use lives in this $k\times d_{\mathrm{in}}$ matrix. Both STU variants then linearly map $Z$ to a $d_{\mathrm{out}}$ -dimensional prediction $y$ .

#### STU.

The STU uses an unconstrained linear map from $\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}$ , parameterized by a tensor $M\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{out}}}$ :

$$ y\;=\;\sum_{k,i}M_{k,i,:}\;Z_{k,i}. $$

Every element of $M$ is independently learned; the map has $k\,d_{\mathrm{in}}\,d_{\mathrm{out}}$ free parameters.

#### Tensor-dot STU.

The tensor-dot variant replaces the single mixer tensor $M\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{out}}}$ with two matrices,

$$ M_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad M_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{out}}}, $$

constraining the mixer to factorize as $M_{k,i,o}=M_{\mathrm{in},k,i}\cdot M_{\mathrm{out},i,o}$ . Two benefits follow.

First, the parameter count drops from $k\,d_{\mathrm{in}}\,d_{\mathrm{out}}$ to $k\,d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{in}}\,d_{\mathrm{out}}$ — at the MuJoCo dimensions $d_{\mathrm{in}}=d_{\mathrm{out}}=128$ and $k=16$ this is a $7.5\times$ reduction.

Second, the factorization permits a cheaper convolutional implementation. In the STU, predicting $y$ involves $k\cdot d_{\mathrm{in}}$ distinct filter convolutions. The tensor-dot factorization lets us instead combine $M_{\mathrm{in}}$ with the spectral filters into $d_{\mathrm{in}}$ per-input-channel filters $f_{:,i}=\sum_{k}M_{\mathrm{in},k,i}\,\phi_{:,k}$ , then perform only $d_{\mathrm{in}}$ time-convolutions (one per input channel) before mixing through $M_{\mathrm{out}}$ . The number of convolutions thus drops from $k\cdot d_{\mathrm{in}}$ to $d_{\mathrm{in}}$ .

However, the tensor-dot STU does have reduced representation capacity, which we analyze in the learning an LDS setting.

## Abstract

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disorder that requires complex treatment decisions and sustained disease self-management. Health literacy is essential for patient understanding of MG, yet online patient education materials (PEMs) have not been systematically studied. This study aimed to evaluate the readability of MG-related PEMs, assess the inclusion of key topics, and identify characteristics associated with more accessible and comprehensive resources.

We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of MG-related PEMs identified through Google and Bing, evaluating readability using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES), Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG). Content analysis was conducted for inclusion of key MG topics. PEMs were categorized by organization type, target population age, and geographic location. Statistical tests included Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis, Mann–Whitney U, and Fisher’s exact test.

All 149 PEMs exceeded the recommended 6th-grade reading level (median FRES 41.8, FKGL 11.4, SMOG 12.9; p < 0.001). Community organization PEMs were more readable than academic PEMs (median FKGL 10.4 vs. 11.6; p = 0.02, median FRES 44.5 vs. 39.4; p = 0.01). Frequently included topics were MG definition (94%), symptoms (93%), and immunotherapy (85%), while medications to avoid (30%), myasthenic crisis (62%), and mental health (10%) were the least included. Readability varied by topic, with immunotherapy and thymectomy sections being the most complex.

MG PEMs are written above recommended readability levels, posing barriers to comprehension. Improving readability and addressing gaps in critical topics, such as medication safety, myasthenic crisis, and mental health could enhance patient understanding and support informed decision-making.

## Introduction

Management of myasthenia gravis (MG) includes increasingly complex immunotherapies [1] and thymectomy [2]. Exacerbations, including myasthenic crisis, remain a major source of morbidity [3]. The burden of the disease has a negative impact on quality of life and mental health and is of substantial concern to patients [4–6]. Patients must engage in complex medical decision-making to manage their risk of high morbidity, making health literacy essential for understanding treatment options and potential disease complications.

Health literacy is commonly defined as the ability to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services in order to make appropriate health decisions [7]. Health literacy is a key determinant of health outcomes in neurologic and chronic conditions. Higher levels of health literacy are associated with better overall health and quality of life in conditions such as spina bifida [8], traumatic brain injury [9], stroke [10], and epilepsy [11, 12]. Health literacy is particularly crucial for self-management skills [13] that are essential in chronic diseases such as MG. Accessible written health information is a central way that health literacy can be supported. When patient education materials (PEMs) are written above patients’ reading levels, they can undermine comprehension and self-management, while revising materials to meet recommended readability levels improves patients’ understanding, supports health literacy and is preferred by patients [14, 15].

The internet is a primary health information source for patients with neurologic conditions at all stages of their disease [16–18] so online PEMs represent an opportunity to advance health literacy. The US Department of Health and Human Services and national organizations such as the American Medical Association and the National Institutes of Health recommend that PEMs should be written below the sixth grade reading level [19]. PEMs written at or below the sixth grade reading level, as measured by readability scores such as the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and the Flesch–Kincaid grade level (FKGL) are associated with improved outcomes, such as decreased readmission rates [20]. However, in various areas of neurology, most PEMs exceed this level [19, 21–28]. The type of organization creating the PEM may affect the readability level [19, 26, 29]. Previous reviews of content addressed in PEMs show that the inclusion of important aspects of the disease varies [19, 22, 28]. An organization’s location may affect the inclusion of key disease-related topics in its PEMs [19]. Online PEMs in neuromuscular disorders, including MG, have not been systematically studied.

This study aims to quantitatively evaluate the readability of online PEMs in MG, review their rates of inclusion of key topics, and identify characteristics that are associated with more readable and more comprehensive PEMs.

## Methods

### Search Strategy

We conducted a cross-sectional readability assessment of PEMs publicly available online. We identified online PEMs about MG available between October 2023 and July 2024 through online search. We conducted the online search by using a single Internet browser (Google Chrome), and we collected the top 200 results on Google (Google LLC, Mountain View, CA, USA) and Bing (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA) with the term “myasthenia + gravis” to approximate patient’s online search for information, similar to prior online PEM reviews [26, 29]. For each PEM, the rank order in each search engine’s search results was documented. If a result appeared in both Google and Bing search results, it was included in the analysis once.

In our search, we did not utilize any search engine filters, such as language or date settings. To eliminate potential influences by search history and location, we erased the Internet browser history, cookies, and cached data. To ensure relevance to our topic of interest, we reviewed each PEM to verify its content contained health information related to MG. If individual links contained linked attachments or secondary pages with additional written educational content, this material was reviewed together with the original page as a single PEM. To avoid overrepresentation from any single source, we included up to two PEMs or links per website for each key topic. The key topic areas are described below in the “Content review” section.

PEMs were included if they contained health information related to MG, were written in English, consisted of at least 100 words or 10 sentences [30], and were freely accessible online. We excluded materials that were not in English, content unrelated to MG (e.g., related to congenital myasthenic syndromes), advertisements without pertinent health information, audio-, video-, or infographic-only materials without accompanying text, non-medical or community-generated content such as patient stories or website and chatroom comments, and materials intended for medical professionals, including journal articles and book chapters. Author ED reviewed all search results for inclusion and exclusion criteria. For results that were ambiguous, the final decision was made by senior author DJC.

Each PEM was categorized according to the type of organization that provided it, age of population referred to and the region where the organization is based. The organization types were divided into four groups: academic, community, government, and industry organizations. Academic sources included universities, medical centers and hospital-affiliated health systems that produced educational materials as part of their clinical or academic mission (e.g., academic neuromuscular centers). Community organizations included patient advocacy groups, foundations and nonprofit organizations that primarily serve patients or caregivers (e.g., MG Foundation of America, Muscular Dystrophy Association). Examples of government and industry sources were public health agencies and pharmaceutical companies respectively. The age of the population was divided into pediatric, adult or both. The regions were categorized as US and non-US, and the US group was further divided into Northeast, Midwest, South and West based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) geographic division [31].

### Text Preparation

The text was prepared according to recommended readability analysis methods [30]. Navigation menus, images, advertisements, periods not marking the end of a sentence, sentence fragments, copyright and/or publication dates, and references were removed and excluded from the analysis. This was done to prevent overestimation of the number of sentences and to maximize the accuracy of the automated text analysis [26, 30]. Each included PEM was prepared and analyzed by one of the authors (ED, AA, AB, or MH) following these methods using Word (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). Any uncertainties during text preparation were resolved by ED, with escalation to senior author DJC when needed.

### Quantitative Readability Analysis

The text, after being formatted for readability analysis, was analyzed with Datayze Readability Analyzer (Datayze, Renton, WA, USA), an online free software that generates descriptive statistics and calculates readability scores and is used by researchers across various fields [19, 32–43]. To compare readability between PEMs, we used FRES, the FKGL, and the Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG) index that are validated scores with established correlation to certain grade reading levels and have been previously used in readability studies in the field of neurology [26, 27, 29].

The FRES index formula generates a score from 0 (most difficult to read) to 100 (easiest to read) based on the average number of words per syllable and number of words per sentence [30]. The score 80–90 indicates that the text is “very easy to read,” suitable for a general audience with a reading level of approximately 6th grade. The validation for this tool was determined by assessing the accuracy of readers in answering multiple-choice question comprehension test with a threshold of 75% correct answers [30, 44].

The FKGL score is a metric that is directly associated with a certain grade based on the Western educational system [45]. It is widely utilized due to its accessibility within Microsoft Word. The index corresponds to the grade level where a reader can score 75% on a comprehension test [30].

The SMOG index indicates the Western grade reading level needed for complete text comprehension so that the reader can answer 100% of questions correctly on a multiple-choice reading comprehension test [30, 46]. It is calculated by assessing 30 sentences of a text, so it can be used on text that is at least 30 sentences long [46]. It is widely used [29, 47], often recommended for use in the health communications [47, 48], and has shown a strong correlation with the required reading level [29].

To compute the readability scores, the analyzer software first extracts several text characteristics including paragraph count, sentence count, and characters per word. The analyzer also reports an additional descriptive metric, the “percentage of difficult words”, that is not part of the FRES, FKGL, or SMOG but is provided as additional information about text complexity. In this metric, “difficult words” are defined as those that are both rare (based on word frequency rankings) and long polysyllabic words with more than three syllables. To calculate this percentage, the software uses a frequency-based “Rare Scale” derived from word recognition studies [49]. Words ranked among the 10,000 most commonly recognized are scored as 0% difficult, while those ranked 20,000 or higher are scored as 100% difficult, with a linear scale applied in between. This measure serves as a proxy for how likely a word is to be recognized and understood by the general public.

### Content Review

To assess the inclusion rates of key topics in PEMs, the following topics were identified in review with neuromuscular colleagues at Montefiore Medical Center along with senior authors DJC and LD as important for clinical care and patient education: Definition and background of MG.Symptoms caused by MG.Myasthenic crisis.Immunotherapy (types and side effects).Thymectomy.Importance of avoidance of medications that can exacerbate myasthenia and where to find a list of these medications.Mental health comorbidities with MG and chronic illnesses.

The topic was considered included if any mention within that topic theme was contained in the text. Each included PEM was reviewed by one of the authors (ED, AA, AB, or MH) for topic inclusion. Any uncertainties were resolved by ED, with escalation to senior author DJC when needed. For the PEMs that had at least one full sentence referring to the key topic, the quantitative data described above were also collected. For each topic, the FRES, FKGL, and SMOG were calculated in addition to paragraph count, sentence count, characters per word, and percentage of difficult words.

### Statistical Analysis

Categorical and dichotomous variables are reported as frequency and percentage. For continuous variables, normality was assessed with histogram inspection, and all continuous variables did not follow a normal distribution. Thus, continuous variables are reported using median and interquartile range (IQR). FRES, FKGL, and SMOG were compared with the recommended reading level of 6th grade using the one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test. To compare the reading scores and text characteristics among all organization types and different areas, the Kruskal–Wallis test was used, and to compare between community and academic organizations and between age of population addressed, the Mann–Whitney U-test was used. To test the proportions of topic inclusion among the organization types and different areas, and between the age groups, the Fisher’s exact test was used. To compare the reading scores with the number of topics included and with the rank order they appeared on the search, the Spearman Rho was used. Based on previously published data (mean FKGL score 12.3, SD 2.25) [19] and our ratio of community vs. academic organizations of 0.6 based on preliminary data, to detect a clinically meaningful difference of 2 in the FKGL score (corresponding to a difference by two grades) between different types of organizations with 80% power, at least 108 unique materials needed to be analyzed. All analyses were performed using STATA/BE 18.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX).

## Results

### Readability Analysis

Our search strategy yielded 188 search results through Google and 200 results through Bing. After removing duplicate results (n = 63) and applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 149 PEMs were included in the final analysis. Of these, 69 appeared only on Google, 44 appeared on Bing, and 36 appeared on both search engines. Details of the screening process are shown in Figure 1.

All PEMs were above the recommended reading level of 6th grade based on all readability formulas (p < 0.001) across all types of organizations (Figure 2). PEMs from community organizations were easier to read compared to academic organizations based on FRES and FKGL. Community-generated PEMs contained more sentences (Table 1).

Readability scores and most text characteristics were similar between PEMs addressing only adult MG and PEMs including information for pediatric patients and caregivers. PEMs that included pediatric information had more sentences compared to PEMs including only adult. Of the included sources 122 (82%) were based in the US. Reading level of PEMs was similar between US and non-US sources. Among the US-based organizations, geographic area was not associated with readability scores. Sources based in the West and Northeast had more paragraphs (Table 1).

Using Bing, the PEMs that appeared higher as search results were more readable (FRES Rho = 0.24, p = 0.04, FKGL Rho = −0.27, p = 0.01, SMOG Rho = −0.28, p = 0.02). Readability was not associated with the rank order of the result in the search through Google.

### Content Inclusion

PEMs included an average of 5 total topics (IQR 4–5) and the rates were similar among the different organization types.

Overall, most PEMs included information about the definition and background of MG (94%), symptoms (93%), immunotherapy (85%), and thymectomy (81%). The topics that were less frequently included were medications that should be avoided in MG (30%) and mental health aspects of the disease (10%) (Table 2 and Figure 3). The total number of topics included was not associated with the reading level of the PEM (FRES p = 0.14, FKGL p = 0.10, SMOG p = 0.55).

PEMs that included information about pediatric MG included more topics and more frequently included information about medications that should be avoided in MG. US organizations from the South CDC division were less likely to include information about thymectomy (Table 2).

Readability varied by topic (Table 3). The passages about mental health were the easiest to read, while the immunotherapy and thymectomy sections were the hardest to read.

## Discussion

All PEMs for MG analyzed in this study are above the recommended reading level of the sixth grade. Most of the PEMs required an 11th grade level to understand 75% of the text, as measured by the FKGL. These findings are consistent with prior literature that shows that PEMs in neurologic conditions are more complex than recommended [19, 21–28]. The lack of readable PEMs presents a major barrier to comprehension, especially for patients with low health literacy, and may limit their ability to understand disease mechanisms, treatment options, and self-management strategies.

PEMs generated by community organizations still exceeded the suggested reading level but were easier to read compared to other organizations, similar to prior studies on PEM readability within neurology [19, 26] and non-neurology areas. In our analysis, there was a 1.2 grade reading level difference compared to academic organizations based on the FKGL. The clinical significance of this is less clear as PEMs from both organization types remained well above the recommended level of 6th grade. In a readability analysis in gynecologic oncology, PEMs generated by pharmaceutical companies were the easiest to read compared to governmental and nonprofit medical associations [50]. In our study, we did not detect this difference; however, we had very few PEMs from industry and government sources compared to academic and community organizations.

Although some organizations recommend an eighth-grade reading level for PEMs, this may overestimate many U.S. adult reading abilities, as national literacy assessments show the majority of Medicaid enrollees read at or below a sixth-grade level [51]. Nearly all PEMs in our sample exceeded the more lenient eighth-grade threshold, indicating that raising the benchmark would not meaningfully alter the conclusion. Notably certain readability scores, for example, SMOG index, may not discriminate as well at lower reading levels, reinforcing the importance of using multiple measures and descriptive text characteristics, as in our analysis, to better capture the complexity of PEMs.

Our study included a content review for inclusion of key topics important to health counseling for MG. Overall safety issues, such as medications that can exacerbate symptoms and should be avoided and information to raise awareness for myasthenic crisis, were included at lower rates. The underrepresentation of these topics raises concerns, as medication-related exacerbations are an easily identifiable and, in most cases, preventable cause of worsening of MG symptoms. Myasthenic crisis is the major source of morbidity and need for hospitalization for individuals living with MG [3]. Comorbid mental health aspects that are a critical component of the health-related quality of life in MG [4–6], were rarely included. Academic and government organizations were more likely to include information about treatment options, such as immunotherapy and thymectomy.

The variation in readability across specific topics also highlights important challenges. Sections discussing immunotherapy and thymectomy were the most difficult to read, despite being central components of MG treatment and counseling. In contrast, mental health content—when present—was written at a much more accessible level, consistent with prior literature [52]. These findings highlight the need to simplify complex treatment information without sacrificing medical accuracy.

Our study complements past work across neurology and neuromuscular diseases [53–56]. A previous readability study in neurologic diseases included a small number of PEMs about MG that were similarly above the recommended reading level [57]. Our approach highlights specific content gaps and readability barriers in MG and certain PEM characteristics that are associated with more readable and comprehensive content.

## Limitations

Our study has a few limitations related to the characteristics of the PEMs identified. We only evaluated English-language PEMs, excluding any audio or video components that may enhance comprehension. We also did not assess materials generated by artificial intelligence (AI), an area for future research given its rapid increase in use across fields. We also excluded content created by individual community members—for example, social media posts—that many patients encounter with health information. Our comparison among organization types was further limited by the relatively small number of PEMs from government and industry sources.

Future research should address these gaps by examining non-English PEMs to better reflect the needs of diverse patient populations. Evaluating multimedia formats, such as video or audio, could offer insight into their potential to improve understanding and engagement. Use of AI technology, particularly generative large language models, has shown promising but mixed results in improving readability of PEMs [58–64]; further studies are needed to assess their reliability, accuracy, and role in patient education. Investigating community-generated content, particularly from social media, is also important given its growing influence on stigma, health beliefs, behaviors, and misconceptions.

There are important limitations stemming from the tools and methods we used. Readability formulas are greatly influenced by polysyllabic words, so MG-related terminology such as “myasthenia,” “thymectomy,” or “autoimmune” can substantially increase the calculated score [65–67]. While these terms may become familiar over the course of an individual’s disease, we cannot assume universal familiarity, especially for those early in the diagnostic process and/or of lower health literacy. Readability metrics only quantify syntactic complexity, not understandability, accuracy, actionability, or trustworthiness. Frameworks such as PEMAT [68], DISCERN [69], or the JAMA Benchmarks [70] may provide complementary evaluations of content quality but were beyond the scope of the study design. Our threshold of topic inclusion may only capture brief or superficial mentions rather than substantive educational content. Future work incorporating a depth-of-coverage scoring and validated quality-assessment tools may offer a more comprehensive PEM quality evaluation. In addition, the key topics were identified by clinicians without direct input from individuals living with MG or caregivers. Incorporating MG-community and -caregiver perspectives could further enhance the relevance and completeness of topic selection and should be an important focus of future work.

## Conclusion

All online PEMs identified for MG are more complex than the recommended reading level and the rates of inclusion of key topics vary. Creating more readable and comprehensive PEMs is needed to improve understanding of the disease for patients living with MG and enhance their participation in shared decision making in their care.
